content: The laryngeal mask airway (LMA) is a reliable and effective device used to maintain the airway during general anaesthesia for surgical procedures. At the conclusion of surgery and anaesthesia, the LMA is removed once the patient demonstrates an adequate respiratory rate and depth. This removal can occur either while the patient is still deeply anaesthetized (referred to as early removal) or after the patient has regained consciousness (referred to as late removal). It remains uncertain which of these two approaches is superior in terms of safety and outcomes. The purpose of this review was to evaluate and compare the safety of removing the LMA during deep anaesthesia (early removal) versus removing it after the patient is awake (late removal) in individuals undergoing general anaesthesia. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, CINAHL, and ISI Web of Science, covering studies up to August 2014. Ongoing trials were identified through trial registration websites, and additional sources such as conference proceedings and reference lists of related articles were also reviewed. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving both adults and children undergoing elective general anaesthesia with the use of the LMA. Studies were eligible if they compared early removal of the LMA (during deep anaesthesia) with late removal (after the patient was awake). Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. A random-effects model was used to analyze the data and generate forest plots. A total of 9188 citations were screened, and 15 RCTs involving 2242 participants were included in the review. The studies primarily used the LMA Classic in patients classified as American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I or II. Eleven trials included children, while five trials focused on adults. However, none of the included studies were of high methodological quality. Eight studies adequately generated random sequences, but only one trial adequately concealed the random sequence. Three trials blinded the outcome assessors. Overall, the majority of the studies had a high risk of bias. Using the GRADE approach, the evidence quality was assessed as low or very low for most outcomes. The risk of laryngospasm was found to be similar between early removal (3.3%) and late removal (2.7%), with a risk ratio (RR) of 1.23 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.74 to 2.03) based on data from 11 trials involving 1615 participants. The evidence quality was very low for the risk of coughing, which was lower with early removal (13.9%) compared to late removal (19.4%), with an RR of 0.52 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.94) from 11 trials involving 1430 participants. The risk of desaturation showed no significant difference between early removal (7.9%) and late removal (10.1%), with an RR of 0.68 (95% CI 0.4 to 1.16) based on 13 trials involving 2037 participants. Low-quality evidence suggested that the risk of airway obstruction was higher with early removal (15.6%) compared to late removal (4.6%), with an RR of 2.69 (95% CI 1.32 to 5.5) from eight trials involving 1313 participants. In conclusion, this systematic review indicates that the current evidence does not demonstrate a clear advantage of either early or late removal of the LMA in patients undergoing general anaesthesia. However, the quality of the available evidence is low or very low, and there is a lack of well-designed RCTs. Further large-scale, high-quality RCTs are needed to determine whether early or late removal of the LMA is superior in terms of safety and clinical outcomes.
